| [THEORY-013](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-013.md) | Once context-dependent marginals are separated from contextuality, the behavioural, social and word-meaning data published as contextual show none | Dzhafarov, Zhang & Kujala (2015), [LIT-264](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-264.md) — Contextuality-by-Default applied to five data sets, including primed word combinations from the quantum-cognition literature. | [THEORY-025](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-025.md) | Neither utility information nor resource holdings, alone or together, can register claims that arise from how differently people convert resources into what they can do and be: equal resources leave unequal capabilities, and utility adapts to deprivation | Sen (1979), [LIT-289](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-289.md), first-hand: a contented disabled person has no marginal-utility claim, no total-utility deficit and no primary-goods deficit, yet an evident claim. The 1998 lecture ([LIT-282](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-282.md)) names four sources of conversion variation. The negative thesis rests on one case and a shared intuition, and Sen says it stands without his positive proposal. The resourcist reply (Pogge) is not held, and the claim does not say capabilities are the right replacement. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-046](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-046.md) v2 | Expected tangible rewards for merely engaging in an interesting task lower later free-choice engagement with it | Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999, [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)): across 55 experiments, expected tangible rewards given for working on an interesting task lowered free-choice engagement after the reward stopped (d = −0.40; children −0.43, college students −0.21), and lowered self-reported interest less (−0.15). By their study-by-study account, Cameron and Pierce's rival analysis found the same for this contingency (performance-independent rewards, −0.29), while disputing nearly everything else. Their 2001 reply (LIT-562), read here, re-codes 145 studies and finds it again: rewards offered for doing an interesting task lowered free choice, −0.35 across 57 studies. Active: both sides of the dispute find this effect. | Active |
| [THEORY-047](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-047.md) | A regulation taken in under controlling conditions is introjected rather than integrated, so the social history of how a value was acquired fixes how autonomous acting on it is | Deci and Ryan ([LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md)) and Ryan and Deci ([LIT-559](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-559.md)): supports for relatedness and competence are enough to get a value internalized, but only as an introject or a compartmentalized identification; integration also needs autonomy support. The experimental evidence is Deci et al. (1994), as reported: the same amount of internalized behaviour correlated positively with felt freedom and enjoyment under autonomy support and negatively under control. Field studies on parenting, religion and medical training agree, correlationally. This is a historical condition on autonomy of the kind [THEORY-040](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-040.md) asks about, with empirical support, but it has not been tested against matched present endorsement or applied to manipulation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-049](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-049.md) v2 | Whether an external event lowers or raises intrinsic motivation depends on whether it is experienced as controlling or as information about competence | Cognitive evaluation theory, as tested by Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999, [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)) and summarized by Ryan and Deci ([LIT-559](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-559.md)) and Deci and Ryan ([LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md)): rewards, feedback, deadlines and choice affect intrinsic motivation through their "functional significance". Controlling events shift the perceived locus of causality outward and undermine it; informational ones affirm competence and enhance it, but only with a sense of autonomy. The meta-analytic pattern fits, and controlling versus informational positive feedback differ by d = −0.78 in four studies. Mediation by felt control is untested for rewards. Its rival, Cameron, Banko and Pierce's account (LIT-562), finds rewards tied to a score or to beating others do not undermine. Neither side has tested mediation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-052](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-052.md) | Frustration of the needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness is a transdiagnostic process in psychopathology | Vansteenkiste, Ryan and Soenens (2020, [LIT-561](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-561.md)) propose that need frustration, distinct from mere lack of satisfaction, plays "a transdiagnostic role", citing a longitudinal study in which it predicted adolescents' depressive and eating symptoms and "largely accounted for their co-occurrence". Deci and Ryan ([LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md)) had located the etiology of "various forms of psychopathology" in developmental need deprivation, with need substitutes, controlled styles and rigid patterns as the route. The evidence is correlational, mostly self-report, and from the theory's authors. A partner of the inflexibility account, not a rival. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-060](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-060.md) | A life story constructed from adolescence on is the form a person's diachronic identity takes, and its content shapes later well-being | McAdams (2019), [LIT-595](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-595.md): narrative identity is "a person's internalized and evolving story of how he or she has become the person he or she is becoming", which gives a life "unity, moral purpose, and temporal coherence". It arrives in adolescence and young adulthood, on the back of autobiographical memory and autobiographical reasoning, as the third layer of a psychological self after the actor of traits and the agent of goals. Stories with agentic and redemptive themes go with well-being and generativity, and in one longitudinal therapy study the story "changes first, and then the storyteller gets better". A review essay: every finding is cited, not shown, and it concedes that having a life story may be a modern cultural construction. Strawson's "Against Narrativity" ([LIT-452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-452.md)) denies the first half for many people. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-074](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-074.md) | Implicit accessibility of the true self-concept is not what self-report scales of authenticity or of need satisfaction measure, though those two self-reports are not shown to be separate constructs | Schlegel, Hicks, Arndt & King (2009), [LIT-606](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-606.md): true-self accessibility, the speed of "me" judgments for traits a person takes to be her true self, correlated .05 with AI-3 authenticity and .20 with basic need satisfaction (N = 124), and each predicted meaning in life independently. The authors read this as showing the constructs differ, and concede the difference is confounded with method, reaction time against self-report. The two self-reports correlated .52, and felt autonomy was only one third of the need-satisfaction composite, whose autonomy items include "I can pretty much be myself". So the paper separates the implicit measure from both self-reports, and does not separate authenticity from autonomy. Proposed: one sample for the correlations, method unresolved. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-077](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-077.md) v2 | Goals pursued for identified or intrinsic reasons receive more sustained effort, which carries their better attainment, and attaining them raises well-being more than attaining goals pursued under pressure | Sheldon & Elliot (1999), [LIT-589](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-589.md): a goal is self-concordant to the degree its reasons are identified or intrinsic rather than external or introjected. In two semester-long student samples, self-concordance predicted sustained effort, and effort fully carried its link to attainment (self-concordance β = .02 and .08, ns, with effort in the model). In the same two samples attainment raised well-being more when goals were self-concordant (interaction β = .11, .23), partly through accumulated daily experiences of autonomy, competence and relatedness. Everything is self-report and correlational, and the structural models fit only after revision. It is evidence for the autonomous end of SDT's continuum, not for integration as distinct from identification. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-123](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-123.md) | In small work groups a member's displayed mood spreads to the others, and the more pleasant mood members catch, the more cooperative and the less conflicted the group; the spread is shown experimentally, its link to group process only by correlation, and members do not credit their mood for how effective they judge themselves | Barsade (2002), [LIT-706](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-706.md), read from the August 2001 manuscript, so every number is the manuscript's. Study 1 (94 undergraduates, 29 groups): a confederate randomly assigned to show pleasant or unpleasant mood moved members' self-reported mood by +.41 or −.26 (χ²(1) = 9.97), and blind video-coders rated members' mood 2.75 against 2.33 (χ²(1) = 10.30). Members who caught more pleasant mood were rated more cooperative, and at group level coder-rated contagion correlated with cooperativeness (r = .44) and against conflict (r = −.42). Study 2 (113 MBA students, 26 groups, no confederate): the ICC of members' mood rose from .00 to .24, and contagion correlated with members' ratings of cooperation (.49) and conflict (−.49). Members related how pleasantly they behaved to others' conduct but showed "absolutely no awareness" of mood bearing on their judged effectiveness. Valence and energy hypotheses failed or were marginal. Proposed: one experiment, one actor, retrospective mood, correlational process effects. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-126](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-126.md) v2 | A collective emotion is the synchronous convergence of individuals' affective responses to one event or object, produced bottom-up by shared appraisal, contagion and group membership, and it needs no group subject; it takes a We-mode form when the appraisals rest on collectively intentional states | von Scheve & Ismer (2013), [LIT-696](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-696.md), a conceptual synthesis with no data: collective emotion is "synchronous convergence in affective responding across individuals towards a specific event or object". Its minimal case is shared appraisal with no mutual awareness (drivers in one traffic jam). Mutual awareness and membership in a collective amplify it, and appraisals grounded in collective intentions give "We-mode" collective emotion, which they expect to differ in quality. Barsade (2002), [LIT-706](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-706.md), supplies the one measured instance: in 26 groups with no confederate, the intraclass correlation of members' mood rose from .00 to .24. The account posits no group subject and does not deny one. Proposed: the definition is stipulated, the routes beyond contagion are untested, and the We-mode clause is a hypothesis its authors say lacks evidence. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-140](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-140.md) | At NASA, as the Columbia Accident Investigation Board found, the Challenger and Columbia accidents had the same organizational cause: evidence that the design was not performing as expected was repeatedly reinterpreted as acceptable, each decision seeming correct in itself and each survived anomaly justifying the next flight, while budget and schedule pressure, consensus sign-off, a hierarchy that kept dissent from rising and a safety organization dependent on the program it oversaw sustained the pattern for twenty years and undid post-Challenger reforms | Columbia Accident Investigation Board (2003), [LIT-734](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-734.md), applying Vaughan's normalization of deviance ([LIT-715](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-715.md), unread). Foam strikes and O-ring erosion followed the same trajectory of incremental acceptance. Organizational culture, structure and political constraint reproduced it, so "history is cause". Proposed: two cases in one agency, reconstructed after the fact, and the general theory is in a book the record has not read. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-142](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-142.md) | Because the returns to exploitation are surer, nearer and closer to the decision than the returns to exploration, organizational learning refines exploitation faster and tends to become self-destructive in the long run; and where an organizational code learns only from members who deviate from it, slow socialization, a mix of slow and fast learners and moderate turnover raise what the organization knows, while without turnover a changing environment degrades its knowledge to chance | March (1991), [LIT-729](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-729.md). Exploration's uncertain, distant returns lose out to exploitation's under learning from experience, trapping organizations in suboptimal equilibria. In a simulation of mutual learning between members and a code, deviation is the code's only source of improvement, so fast socialization hurts the organization and moderate turnover helps it. Proposed: the dynamics are shown only in a stylized model, and the trade-off is argued, not measured. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-144](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-144.md) | Under steady cost and effort pressure, an organization's activity migrates toward the boundary of acceptable performance, and redundant defences erode unobserved because a breach of one shows no effect, so that major accidents arise from many locally reasonable decisions rather than from coincident errors | Rasmussen (1997), [LIT-743](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-743.md). Within a work space bounded by functional, administrative and safety constraints, a cost gradient from management and an effort gradient from the work drive activity toward the boundary. Defence in depth hides the drift, and accidents such as Zeebrügge are prepared by decision makers each optimising locally. Proposed: the account is built from accident reconstructions, which see only the cases that crossed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-145](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-145.md) | Organizations that espouse revising their governing values characteristically fail to, because the theory-in-use people actually act on keeps premises tacit and tests self-sealing, and the resulting defensive routines make the inconsistency, and its undiscussability, undiscussable; so errors are corrected within the governing values (single-loop) while the values themselves go unexamined | Argyris (2002), [LIT-745](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-745.md). Single-loop learning corrects errors within governing values; double-loop learning changes them. People espouse the second but act on Model I (control, winning, suppressing negative feelings, appearing rational). Defensive routines then make the gap undiscussable, and individual and organizational routines reinforce each other. Proposed: the evidence is the author's own workshops, and the universality claim is asserted from earlier work. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-149](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-149.md) | Users can govern a shared resource durably without either privatisation or central control, and the institutions that last are marked not by particular rules but by structural regularities: user-made and user-monitored rules, graduated sanctions, cheap local conflict resolution, recognised rights to self-organise, and nested layers of governance | Ostrom's account, read in her Nobel lecture ([LIT-719](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-719.md)). Coded case meta-analyses, laboratory and field experiments and multi-country field studies agree that resource users often self-govern successfully. Long-surviving institutions share eight design principles that failed ones lack. The principles are correlates of survival, not tested causes, and their reach beyond common-pool resources is not shown. | Active |
| [THEORY-152](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-152.md) | When a firm, public service or other organization deteriorates, its members' exit and voice are both recuperation mechanisms: voice carries richer information than exit and can be felt as a benefit rather than a cost, exit can be costly even without loyalty and can signal nothing, loyalty makes members voice rather than exit, and an organization needs floor levels of both for feedback but disintegrates or is disrupted beyond ceiling levels, while its managers may favour whichever response least threatens their hold on power | Hirschman (1974; Milbank reprint 1980), [LIT-750](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-750.md), revisiting his 1970 book ([LIT-748](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-748.md), unread). Exit and voice are the two ways members respond to decline and the two channels of feedback. Voice deserves more weight than the book gave it; exit is neither free nor always informative; managers manage both. Proposed: argued from examples, and loyalty's role is presupposed from the book rather than developed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-153](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-153.md) | A system can keep its identity independently within a shared environment only if it has five interacting subsystems, the first made of elements that are themselves viable systems, so that the structure recurs at every level of recursion; when one is missing or fails, the system degrades in characteristic ways, and without the subsystem for foresight the subsystems for operational control and for identity collapse into each other, leaving a system that can only react | Beer's Viable System Model, as he states it in his 1984 retrospective [LIT-752](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-752.md). Five subsystems are necessary and sufficient for any organism or organization to maintain its identity independently; every viable system contains and is contained in one; breakdowns trace to a failing subsystem. Proposed: the paper declines to validate the model, the evidence is the author's consultancy, and no observation the model forbids is named. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-154](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-154.md) | Whether an expected tangible reward lowers or raises later intrinsic motivation depends on how tightly its stated contingency ties it to performance and success | Cameron, Banko and Pierce (2001, [LIT-562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-562.md)), re-analysing 145 studies with contingencies coded by procedure. On interesting tasks, expected tangible rewards undermine later free choice when loosely tied to performance (for doing the task, for "doing well") or earned at less than the maximum; they do not when given for surpassing a score, and they enhance it when given for exceeding others. Read through social cognitive and behavioural theory: rewards tied to success carry competence. Proposed: the paper measures no mediator and pools control groups that differ in feedback. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-164](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-164.md) | In groups that build a new communication system, larger groups make it more systematic, and the greater variety of input they face drives the effect | Raviv, Meyer & Lev-Ari (2019), [LIT-825](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-825.md), read in [NOTE-628](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-628.md): fully connected groups of eight built more systematic languages than groups of four, faster and more uniformly, with total interaction and network structure fixed; input variability, larger in bigger groups, predicted the gains. One laboratory study, two group sizes, and a mechanism supported by lagged association, not manipulation. It says nothing yet about natural communities, where size travels with network density and second-language learners. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-166](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-166.md) | Survey question-order effects leave the probability of giving the same answer to both questions unchanged, as a projection model predicts, and this regularity does not by itself favour quantum over classical probability | Wang, Solloway, Shiffrin & Busemeyer (2014), [LIT-795](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-795.md), on the QQ equality derived in [LIT-834](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-834.md): across 66 unselected Pew surveys, question order shifts the answers (p = 0.0004) but not the probability that the two answers agree (p = 0.4625). The Lüders projection model predicts this without parameters. The authors concede that a classical model can be built to satisfy the equality, and [LIT-264](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-264.md) shows that data meeting it are noncontextual, so it is evidence for a constraint on order effects, not for nonclassical probability or contextuality. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-167](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-167.md) | The Russian wondertale is built from a small fixed set of character functions in a fixed order, so that all wondertales share one composition and differ in who performs the functions and how | Propp (1928), [LIT-828](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-828.md), read in [NOTE-615](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-615.md): in Afanasyev's tales 50–151 the constant elements are 31 functions of characters, defined by their consequence for the action, occurring in one order and falling to seven roles. One analyst, one corpus of a hundred tales, and a class of "wondertales" redefined in the end as the tales that follow the scheme. It does not say all folktales, or all narratives, share the structure, and the claims of a single source tale and of mythic origin are conjectures the book does not support. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-173](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-173.md) | Large models are a cultural and social technology rather than agents: lossy, uninvertible summaries of human-produced information that, like prices and bureaucratic categories, let it be reorganized at scale | Farrell, Gopnik, Shalizi & Evans (2025), [LIT-848](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-848.md), read in [NOTE-649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-649.md). A classification argued by analogy with print, markets, bureaucracies and elections, with one mechanism (fit to the average makes models worst on rare cases, which may homogenize culture). Proposed: no evidence is offered, and the paper gives no criterion by which the classification could fail. | Proposed |
